newsitem.title: USA: Treasure hunters in Florida court over seabed damage.
newsitem.headline: Treasure hunters in Florida court over seabed damage.

text.p: Two Florida treasure hunters who discovered riches in a sunken Spanish galleon appeared in court on Tuesday to face a government lawsuit that could force them to turn over the booty and pay $600,000 in environmental damages.

Five years ago a salvage company run by Mel Fisher and his son Kane discovered the San Fernando galleon, which sank off the Florida Keys in 1733. They recovered more than 200 artifacts, including an iron cannon, musket balls, silver coins and gold bullion.

Government lawyers said the Kanes' three-month treasure-hunting expedition took a tremendous toll on the ocean bed. The salvage ships used two L-shaped pipes to blow propellor wash into sand and sea grasses. They allegedly dug 597 craters, some as deep as nine feet (three metres) and as wide as 40 feet (13 metres).
All told more than 1.6 acres (6,470 square metres) of sea grass were killed, the government says.
Government lawyers said the entire operation was illegal because it took place within the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a 2,800-square mile (7,252 sq km) reserve established in 1990.

"This case is basically about accountability to the public for the taking of public resources," attorney James Lofton, who heads the case for the U.S. Justice Department, said on Tuesday, the second day of the trial.
Mel Fisher says the government is trying to take what is rightfully his -- booty from a ship that sank in international waters before the United States even existed.
"This is another attempt by the federal government to grab the treasure," he said outside court on Tuesday.
Fisher, 74, also downplayed the environmental damage from treasure hunting.

"It's much like a farmer cultivating his field. When the soil is turned over it makes everything much better. Before I got there it was like a barren desert. Now there are sea fans and other marine life."

Throughout much of the Florida Keys, vast stretches of sea grass have been scarred by boats racing across the shallow flats. The government wants Fisher to pay $589,331 for a massive seagrass restoration in the San Fernando search area because the currents are thought to be too strong for transplanted grass to take hold.

Government witness Jay Zieman, a tropical seagrass expert from the University of Virginia, said it would take 50 to 100 years for nature to replace the sea grasses. Fisher's expert is expected to argue that the grasses will grow back much quicker.
The case, heard without a jury, is expected to last several weeks. Fisher's lawyers will argue it is impossible to tell whether the craters were caused by natural currents, other hunters or Fisher.
"This week the plaintiffs have their expert witnesses up. Next week it's our turn at bat," Fisher's spokesman Pat Clyne said.
